analysis.one_liner: Gives 401(k) workers the right to sell off company stock and requires notice when trading is frozen.
analysis.headline: The House Ways and Means Committee approved the bill by voice vote in March 2002 and placed it on the House calendar, but it never came up for a floor vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Enron collapse wiped out employees' 401(k) savings that were locked into company stock, this bill would have given retirement plan participants a right to sell company stock out of their accounts — starting with 20% a year in 2003 and reaching 100% by 2007. It also required plans to offer at least three investment options other than company stock, to send plain-language investment education notices each quarter, and to warn workers at least 30 days before a 'blackout' period when they could not trade, with a $100-per-worker tax on plans that failed. A separate title exempted stock-option gains from payroll taxes, and other titles reduced pension-insurance premiums for small employers and eased paperwork.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose 401(k) accounts are heavily invested in their employer's stock — roughly tens of millions of 401(k) participants — gain the right to diversify out of it, starting with one-fifth of their employee contributions each year and phasing to all of it by 2007. All plan participants gain quarterly plain-language investment education notices and 30-day advance warning of transaction restriction (blackout) periods, backed by a $100-per-participant excise tax when plans fail to provide them. Small-business owners gain lower pension-insurance premiums and simplified reporting.

how_it_helps.text: Workers in plans holding employer stock can elect to move up to 20% of employee contributions out of company stock in 2003, rising to 100% in 2007 and later, and plans must offer at least three investment options other than employer securities with elections allowed at least quarterly.
Plans must warn participants at least 30 days before a transaction restriction (blackout) period begins, including blackouts tied to employer securities, or pay a $100-per-participant tax.

Plans must provide quarterly plain-language notices explaining diversification and the risk of holding large amounts of one company's stock — the mistake that cost Enron employees their retirement savings.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and plan sponsors bear the cost of quarterly notices, blackout warnings, and offering non-company-stock options, and companies that keep employee retirement savings in their own stock lose that captive pool. The Treasury forgoes payroll tax revenue from the stock-option exemption in Title III, with Social Security and Medicare trust funds made whole from other revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, plan sponsors, and the Treasury

drawbacks.text: The stock-option title (Title III) exempts incentive stock option and employee stock purchase plan gains from Social Security, Medicare, and unemployment payroll taxes and from wage withholding, a tax break that flows mostly to option-granting companies and their higher-paid employees.

Diversification rights phase in slowly — only 20% of employee-contribution holdings could be sold in 2003, and company stock held as employer matches was locked until a worker had three years of service — and collectively bargained plans get a delayed effective date.
The notice penalties are gentle: taxes are capped at $500,000 per year for unintentional failures, can be avoided by correcting within 30 days, and can be waived by the Treasury Secretary.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — a worker's right to sell company stock out of a retirement account and advance warning of trading blackouts — directly addresses what destroyed Enron employees' savings, and the cost to employers is compliance paperwork rather than anything structural. The weaknesses are the slow phase-in, the soft penalties, and a Title III payroll-tax break for stock options that has little to do with the worker-protection purpose and mostly benefits option-heavy companies and better-paid employees.

outcome.mechanism: The House Ways and Means Committee approved it by voice vote and it was placed on the House calendar in April 2002, but House leaders never brought it up for a vote — a competing pension bill moved instead — and it died when the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Rob Portman introduced the bill on February 4, 2002, together with Rep. Benjamin Cardin, a bipartisan pairing.
The House Ways and Means Committee considered and marked up the bill on March 14, 2002, ordered it reported as amended by voice vote, and reported it on March 20 with House Report 107-382.
On April 9, 2002 the Education and Workforce Committee was discharged from further consideration and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar — the list of bills awaiting a House floor vote.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a House floor vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that keep 401(k) savings in their own company stock, and companies granting stock options, are better off because the bill died: they never faced mandatory diversification rights or the option payroll-tax change. Workers got no federal right to diversify from this bill; narrower blackout-notice rules did pass later in 2002 in the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, but the broader diversification rights did not.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers holding worker savings in company stock

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — a Republican lead sponsor with a Democratic co-introducer and 21 cosponsors split 15 Republicans and 6 Democrats — and the Ways and Means Committee reported it by voice vote, with no recorded opposition anywhere in the House.

industries.industry: Employers sponsoring 401(k) plans that hold their own stock
industries.note: The bill would force companies to let employees sell company stock out of their accounts and to offer alternative investments, ending the practice of keeping worker retirement savings locked in employer stock — the mechanism that wiped out Enron workers. Companies comply through paperwork and lost control of a captive pool of capital.

industries.industry: Companies granting stock options (especially tech firms)
industries.note: Title III exempts incentive stock option and employee purchase plan gains from payroll taxes and withholding, cutting costs for option-heavy employers and for their option-holding employees, while the Treasury loses revenue. It benefits higher-paid option holders more than rank-and-file workers.

Mandatory diversification rights would push employee money out of single-company stock and into the required non-employer investment options, and the bill's tax treatment encourages employer-provided retirement planning services.

industries.industry: Small employers with defined benefit plans
industries.note: The bill cuts new-plan Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation premiums to $5 per participant for small employers and caps variable premiums for very small plans, easing the cost of offering pensions — though lower premiums shift somewhat more risk onto the federal pension backstop.
